title: Linux Process Control: ps, Signals and systemd
summary: Quick revision notes on inspecting processes with ps and top, managing jobs, sending signals, reading exit codes, and running services with systemd and journalctl.

chapters.title: Process Mental Model
points: A process is a running program with a PID and a PPID (parent). Every process is started by a parent, and PID 1 (init/systemd) is the ancestor of all of them
Process states in the STAT column: R running, S sleeping, D uninterruptible I/O wait (cannot be killed), T stopped, Z zombie (exited, parent has not called wait)
Foreground jobs own the terminal. Background jobs run detached from the keyboard, but they still die with the shell on hangup unless protected by nohup or disown
Control layers, from low to high: the signal (the kernel's message to a process), the job (a shell-level handle on a process), the service (a systemd-supervised process with logs and restart policy)
Interview Point: What is the difference between a zombie and an orphan process? Why can't kill -9 remove a zombie? What does PID 1 do for orphans?

chapters.title: Inspecting Processes with ps and top
points: ps shows a one-time snapshot; top refreshes live. Use ps for scripting and top for watching load
ps aux lists all users' processes in BSD style: USER PID %CPU %MEM VSZ RSS STAT COMMAND. ps -ef shows PPID and the full command line in POSIX style
Filter with ps -p PID, pgrep -a name, or ps aux | grep [n]ginx. The [n] bracket trick stops grep from matching itself
top keys: P sort by CPU, M sort by memory, k kill a PID, 1 show per-core CPU, q quit. The load average shows 1, 5 and 15 minute values, and a load above the core count means saturation
Interview Point: What do VSZ and RSS mean, and which one tells you real memory use? How do you find which process is using the most memory? What does load average measure?

chapters.title: Jobs: Foreground and Background
points: cmd & starts a job in the background. Ctrl+Z suspends the foreground job (SIGTSTP), and Ctrl+C interrupts it (SIGINT)
jobs lists the shell's jobs with numbers like [1]+. fg %1 brings job 1 to the foreground, and bg %1 resumes a stopped job in the background
Standard workflow: run a long command, press Ctrl+Z, run bg to keep it running, then run fg to return to it
Closing the terminal sends SIGHUP and kills background jobs. Prevent that with nohup cmd & (its output goes to nohup.out), or disown -h %1 for a job that is already running
Interview Point: How do you move a running foreground command into the background? Why do jobs die when the SSH session closes, and how do you stop that? What is the difference between jobs and ps?

chapters.title: Signals, kill and Exit Codes
points: kill PID sends SIGTERM (15) by default. SIGTERM can be caught, so the process can clean up and exit. kill -9 sends SIGKILL, which cannot be caught or ignored and gives no cleanup
Common signals: 1 HUP (reload config or hangup), 2 INT (Ctrl+C), 9 KILL, 15 TERM, 18 CONT (resume), 19 STOP (pause, uncatchable), 20 TSTP (Ctrl+Z)
killall name and pkill -f pattern kill by name or by full command line. Always preview with pgrep -a first, because pattern matching can hit unrelated processes

Exit code 0 means success and nonzero means failure. $? holds the last command's code. 126 is not executable, 127 is command not found, and 128+N means killed by signal N (137 = SIGKILL, 143 = SIGTERM)
Interview Point: Why try SIGTERM before SIGKILL? What does exit code 137 tell you in a container or service? How do you check whether the last command succeeded?

chapters.title: systemd Services and journalctl
points: systemd is PID 1 and manages services defined in unit files such as /etc/systemd/system/app.service. Key sections: [Unit] ordering, [Service] ExecStart, User and Restart=on-failure, [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target

Lifecycle commands: systemctl start|stop|restart|reload|status app. enable makes it start at boot and disable removes that. enable --now does enable and start together. The two are independent: start does not enable, and enable does not start
After editing a unit file, run systemctl daemon-reload, or systemd keeps using the old definition. List failures with systemctl --failed
journalctl -u app shows a service's logs. Useful flags: -f follow live, -n 100 last 100 lines, --since '1 hour ago', -p err only errors and worse, -b current boot only
Interview Point: What is the difference between restart and reload? Why does a service not start at boot after systemctl start? How do you debug a service that keeps crashing?

chapters.title: Process Control Cheat Sheet
points: Inspect: ps aux, ps -ef, pgrep -a name, top (P, M, 1, k, q), and STAT letters R S D T Z
Jobs: cmd &, Ctrl+Z, jobs, bg %n, fg %n, nohup cmd &, disown -h %n
Signals: kill PID (15), kill -9 (last resort), kill -HUP (reload), pkill -f pattern, killall name
Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 general error, 126 not executable, 127 not found, 130 Ctrl+C, 137 SIGKILL, 143 SIGTERM, read with $?

systemd: systemctl start|stop|restart|status|enable --now|daemon-reload, journalctl -u app -f -n 100 --since -p err. Interview Point: When do you use enable versus start, and what do 137 and 143 each mean?
